scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Jhum dance is inextricably linked to the history of the Tripuri people, who constitute over half of the tribal population in the state of Tripura.
Historically, these communities lived in the hills and practiced shifting cultivation.
The dance evolved as a celebratory response to the successful completion of various stages of the jhum cycle.
on_screen: Map: India · South Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed during annual regional celebrations that revolve around the agricultural seasons, specifically sowing and harvesting.
It is a communal celebration of the 'jhum' lifestyle.
For the participants, the dance is a way to honor the land and ensure a bountiful harvest, often coinciding with festivals like Garia Puja or Mamita.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Jhum dance is typically performed by groups of girls and boys.

While specific step-by-step choreography is not detailed in the primary sources, it follows the general pattern of Tripuri folk dances which involve rhythmic movements often synchronized with the beat of drums and flutes.
In related regional dances like the Garia, the tempo gradually increases, and dancers use mudras (gestures) that mimic nature, suggesting a similar energetic and mimetic quality in the Jhum dance.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music accompanying the Jhum dance is provided by traditional instruments common to the Tripura hills.
These include the khamb (a type of drum), the flute, and the sarinda.
Listen for the Khamb, Flute, Sarinda, Pung.

The sound is dominated by the deep, rhythmic pulse of the khamb drum and the melodic overlays of the bamboo flute. The music is designed to build energy, starting at a steady pace and accelerating to a climax that mirrors the excitement of the harvest.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers perform in the open air, typically within village squares or near agricultural fields during festival times.
Women adorn themselves with traditional silver jewelry, including chains, rings, and bangles, as well as bronze ear and nose rings.
The attire is colorful and reflects the ethnic identity of the specific clan or tribe, such as the Tripuri or Marma peoples.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The sources do not name individual historical choreographers, as the Jhum dance is a collective folk tradition passed down through oral and physical practice within the Tripuri and Marma communities.
While the Jhum dance is a distinct form, it exists within a cluster of related tribal dances in Tripura.
The Jhum dance belongs to the indigenous folk lineage of the Tibeto-Burman speaking tribes of Northeast India.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Jhum dance is sibling of Garia dance: Both are agricultural dances of the Tripuri people performed during the sowing season.
Jhum dance is sibling of Lebang Boomani: A harvest-time dance involving the catching of insects, sharing the same musical ensemble.
